Chinese Threat Actor Uses Leaked DarkSword Kit to Deploy GHOSTBLADE on iOS

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An unknown Chinese-threat actor has been observed running a campaign targeting Apple iOS devices by leveraging a publicly leaked version of the DarkSword exploit kit. Attack surface management platform Censys said it identified the threat actor running more than 100 web properties, most of which are fake Amazon Web Services (AWS) sign-in pages on a domain that also hosts the exploit toolkit. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Managed device egress to DarkSword/GHOSTBLADE watering-hole & Apple-ID decoy hosts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Device beaconing to DarkSword operator panels (DarkSword Admin / Decode Dashboard / C2) on 8888,3000 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Managed device egress to DarkSword/GHOSTBLADE watering-hole & Apple-ID decoy hosts AIDelivery High
Hunts any corporate/managed (especially iOS) device making an outbound web connection to the two hosts serving the DarkSword campaign's AWS-console impersonation and Apple ID credential-harvest decoys, which front the exploit-delivery iframe. A hit means a device reached the initial-access lure that fires the DarkSword chain against iOS 18.4–18.7. Rationale: Uses the two article/Censys-identified entry hosts (38.181.52.95 = exploit-toolkit/exploit-panel front ends; 103.106.190.217 = Apple ID decoy co-hosting C2 Control Panel). These are dedicated malicious hosts, so any managed-device contact is high-fidelity; DeviceInfo join surfaces whether the device is iOS 18.x (the DarkSword target band). Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/darksword-ios-exploit-chain • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-darksword-ios-exploit-used-in-infostealer-attack-on-iphones/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/darksword-ios-exploit-kit-uses-6-flaws.html
ATT&CKT1189 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst or TIP enrichment box actively browsing the reported infrastructure
  • Automated URL/sandbox detonation appliance detonating campaign IOCs
  • Vulnerability scanner or ASM tool reaching out to the hosts
  • IP reallocation: 103.106.190.217/38.181.52.95 later reassigned to a benign tenant after takedown
  • Corporate egress-proxy health check probing a blocklisted IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","ti-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source device and confirm it is a real endpoint (not a TI/sandbox host); pull OSPlatform/OSVersion — an iOS 18.4–18.7 device is the intended victim. Check what URL/host was requested (RemoteUrl) for the AWS-console or Apple ID decoy path. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the perimeter/MDM egress, isolate/force-reboot the affected iPhone (GHOSTBLADE is memory-only, so reboot disrupts the implant), and force an Apple ID password reset + revoke sessions for the user. 3) Hunt: pivot the same device/user to UC-2 (operator panel IPs on 8888/3000) for exfil, and review Entra/iCloud sign-ins from the device's egress IP for post-compromise credential reuse.
let DeliveryIPs = dynamic(["38.181.52.95","103.106.190.217"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (DeliveryIPs)
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, OSVersion) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let DeliveryIPs = dynamic(["38.181.52.95","103.106.190.217"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in (DeliveryIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f2b1c84-9d3e-4a71-8b0f-2e5c7a11d904

Device beaconing to DarkSword operator panels (DarkSword Admin / Decode Dashboard / C2) on 8888,3000 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from any managed device to the DarkSword operator infrastructure — DarkSword Admin, Decode Dashboard, and C2 Control Panel login/staging IPs (largely on non-standard ports 8888/3000). This is the GHOSTBLADE exfiltration/C2 leg where harvested keychain, iCloud and Wi-Fi credentials are shipped to attacker endpoints. Rationale: Uses the full Censys-published operator panel/staging IP set — DarkSword Admin (:8888: 38.22.89.117, 103.97.128.67, 162.4.136.30, 223.26.63.56, 151.243.126.191; :3000: 107.175.49.181, 103.238.129.112), Decode Dashboard (103.226.155.200/.201, 202.8.120.249), C2 Control Panel (103.106.190.217), and the Frankfurt open-directory tooling host (93.152.221.37). These are single-purpose adversary panels, so any device beaconing to them — flagged especially on the observed 8888/3000 ports — is a strong exfil/C2 signal. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/darksword-ios-exploit-chain • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-darksword-ios-exploit-used-in-infostealer-attack-on-iphones/ • https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/darksword-iphone-exploit-spies-thieves
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/TI analyst enumerating the operator panels for research
  • Sandbox or crawler detonating the IOCs
  • ASM/attack-surface scanner probing ports 8888/3000 across these hosts
  • Post-takedown IP reallocation to a benign host still on the blocklist
  • Internal tooling on a shared VPS range coincidentally sharing an IP after reassignment
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","ti-","scanner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is a genuine endpoint and check RemotePort — 8888/3000 to these IPs is the operator-panel shape; bytes-out volume indicates whether this is a login gate probe vs. a bulk credential upload. Correlate the same device against UC-1 (decoy-host contact) within the prior hours. 2) Contain: block all listed IPs at perimeter/MDM egress, isolate/reboot the iPhone, and immediately rotate + revoke Apple ID, iCloud, and any Wi-Fi/enterprise creds reachable from that device (GHOSTBLADE dumps keychain/iCloud/Wi-Fi). 3) Hunt: sweep all egress logs org-wide for any other device touching these IPs or t.me/YATA0000, and review Entra/iCloud sign-ins originating from the operator IP ranges for stolen-credential reuse.

| order by Timestamp desc
let OperatorPanelIPs = dynamic(["38.22.89.117","103.97.128.67","162.4.136.30","223.26.63.56","151.243.126.191","107.175.49.181","103.238.129.112","103.226.155.200","103.226.155.201","202.8.120.249","103.106.190.217","93.152.221.37"]);

| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",

Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-08-03 11 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Non-Chrome process connects to Google cloud authenticator enclave.ua5v.com (Pass-ta-key) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Chrome process reads Google synced-passkey store (Sync Data LevelDB) or device identity key · [LLM] Deletion of Chrome passkey_enclave_state forcing UV-key re-onboarding (Silver Pass-ta-key) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Non-Chrome process reads Google synced-passkey store (Sync Data LevelDB) or device identity key AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a process other than Chrome creating, copying, modifying or renaming files inside Chrome's synced-passkey LevelDB store, where WebauthnCredentialSpecifics records (usernames, credential IDs, encrypted private keys) live. This is the Stage-Zero reconnaissance / Golden Pass-ta-key extraction step: malware reads or copies the store to enumerate and steal synced passkeys without elevation. Rationale: Uses the exact article path %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\Sync Data\LevelDB where WebauthnCredentialSpecifics live; only Chrome/GoogleUpdate legitimately touch this store, so any other writer is high-fidelity. Path and WebauthnCredentialSpecifics store confirmed by Unit42 Part 2 and independent write-ups (cybersecuritynews, gbhackers). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-authenticators-hidden-passkey-architecture/ • https://gbhackers.com/google-authenticators-passkey/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup/DLP agent snapshotting the whole Chrome profile directory
  • Security/EDR tooling or forensic collectors (e.g. velociraptor, KAPE) reading browser artifacts
  • Chrome profile migration or sync-repair utilities run by IT
  • Antivirus real-time scanner opening/quarantining LevelDB files (may surface as rename)
  • Legitimate browser-data importer tools during onboarding of a new browser
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe","backup.exe","CrowdStrike","velociraptor.exe","kape.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/FolderPath and SHA256; confirm it is not a signed backup/EDR/IT tool and whether it is user-writable (Temp, AppData, Downloads). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and force a Google account sign-out plus passkey re-enrollment for the affected user; revoke synced-device trust in the Google account. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same binary hash org-wide, look for follow-on connections to enclave.ua5v.com (UC3) and deletion of passkey_enclave_state (UC2), and check for exfil of copied LevelDB files.
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and FolderPath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB" | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","msedge.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessTokenElevation, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" and TargetFilePath has @"\Sync Data\LevelDB" | where ActingProcessName !has "chrome.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "GoogleUpdate.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "elevation_service.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "software_reporter_tool.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "msedge.exe" | where ActorUsername !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName | order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Chrome Process Writes to Google Passkey Sync LevelDB Store
id: b3f1c2a4-1d2e-4f6a-9c11-7a2b3c4d5e6f
status: experimental
description: Detects a non-Chrome process creating/modifying files in the Chrome synced-passkey LevelDB store (WebauthnCredentialSpecifics), as abused by Unit42 Pass-ta-key passkey theft.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication-security-risks/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.003
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:

  filter_chrome:

      - '\GoogleUpdate.exe'
      - '\elevation_service.exe'
      - '\software_reporter_tool.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_chrome
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*Sync?Data\\LevelDB* OR @TargetFilename:*Sync?Data\\leveldb*) NOT (@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\GoogleUpdate.exe OR *\\elevation_service.exe OR *\\software_reporter_tool.exe OR *\\msedge.exe))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten | TargetFileName=/\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\.*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\/i | ContextImageFileName!=/\\(chrome|GoogleUpdate|elevation_service|software_reporter_tool|msedge)\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*") AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","msedge.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\*\\Sync Data\\LevelDB\\*") AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","msedge.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Deletion of Chrome passkey_enclave_state forcing UV-key re-onboarding (Silver Pass-ta-key) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a non-Chrome process deleting, renaming or modifying the Chrome passkey_enclave_state file, which stores the device-onboarding trust state (identity + user-verification keys). Wiping it forces Chrome to re-onboard, the pivot the Silver Pass-ta-key attack uses to inject an attacker-controlled UV key and fake biometric device-unlock. Rationale: Targets the exact article/Part-2 artifact passkey_enclave_state (confirmed at %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\passkey_enclave_state by independent write-ups); its deletion/rename by anything but Chrome forces device re-onboarding, the precondition for the Silver Pass-ta-key attacker-controlled UV-key injection. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-authenticators-hidden-passkey-architecture/
ATT&CKT1556 T1111
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User clears Chrome browsing data / resets Chrome profile
  • IT re-provisioning or roaming-profile cleanup deleting the Chrome profile
  • Antivirus quarantining the file (surfaces as delete/rename)
  • Chrome self-repair or version upgrade rewriting enclave state
  • Disk-cleanup / privacy tools (CCleaner-style) wiping browser artifacts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe","cleanmgr.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the deleting process is not chrome.exe/IT tooling and check for a fresh onboarding immediately after (new identity/UV key registration) — a delete followed by re-onboard is the attack signature. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the offending binary, and suspend the Google account + revoke device trust so the re-onboarded (attacker) device cannot assert. 3) Hunt: correlate with subsequent enclave.ua5v.com traffic from non-Chrome (UC3) and reads of the Sync Data LevelDB store (UC1) on the same host/user.
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileModified","FileRenamed") | where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" | where FileName has "passkey_enclave_state" | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","msedge.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessTokenElevation, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventType in ("FileDeleted","FileModified","FileRenamed") | where TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\" | where TargetFileName has "passkey_enclave_state" | where ActingProcessName !has "chrome.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "GoogleUpdate.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "elevation_service.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "msedge.exe" | where ActorUsername !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName | order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-Chrome process connects to Google cloud authenticator enclave.ua5v.com (Pass-ta-key) AICommand & Control High
Hunts network/DNS activity to the Google cloud authenticator domain enclave.ua5v.com originating from any process other than Chrome. Legitimate passkey operations reach this enclave only via chrome.exe; a foreign process talking to it indicates malware impersonating the device identity key to silently sign authentication challenges (the core Pass-ta-key / Silver Pass-ta-key account-takeover step). Rationale: enclave.ua5v.com is the Google Password Manager cloud-authenticator endpoint (confirmed by independent Part-2 coverage); only chrome.exe legitimately connects, so a non-Chrome process reaching it is a near-unambiguous signal of device-identity impersonation / forged passkey assertions. Sentinel field left empty because this tenant's Sentinel schema exposes only host-level DNS (DnsEvents) with no process attribution, which cannot separate malware from Chrome; process-attributed detection is delivered via Defender/Sysmon/FDR. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/google-authenticators-hidden-passkey-architecture/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/passwordless-authentication/
ATT&CKT1606 T1550
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome-based wrapper apps (Electron/CEF) that legitimately use Google passkey APIs but ship a renamed binary
  • Enterprise proxy/inspection agent re-originating the TLS connection to enclave.ua5v.com
  • Security tooling performing domain reputation lookups against ua5v.com
  • New Chrome channel (Beta/Dev/Canary) whose binary name differs from chrome.exe
  • Automated browser test frameworks (Selenium/Playwright driving a non-chrome.exe driver)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedgewebview2.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating binary/path/hash and confirm it is not a signed Chromium-based app or proxy agent; a user-writable-path process contacting enclave.ua5v.com is high-severity. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the process, suspend the Google account and revoke synced-device trust to invalidate any forged assertions. 3) Hunt: on the same host/user look back for reads of the Sync Data LevelDB store (UC1) and deletion of passkey_enclave_state (UC2), and review Google account activity for logins with no corresponding device-unlock/biometric.
DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where RemoteUrl has "enclave.ua5v.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".ua5v.com" | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort | order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where RemoteUrl has "enclave.ua5v.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".ua5v.com" | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort | order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

PNLD Breach Exposes U.K. Police and Government Contact Details on Dark Web

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Police National Legal Database (PNLD) has confirmed that police, government and customer contact information was compromised and published on the dark web. The data included names, organisations and work email addresses belonging to police officers, police staff, criminal justice professionals, government partners and customers. The incident, identified on July 26, also exposed some names

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1566 T1566.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Dataverse table enumeration across Power Pages /_api and /_odata entity sets
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound phishing leveraging the PNLD / ExfilSquad breach against named officers · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anonymous bulk Dataverse extraction via Power Pages Web API / legacy OData feed · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Anonymous bulk Dataverse extraction via Power Pages Web API / legacy OData feed AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts high-volume, successful requests to Microsoft Power Pages Web API ('/_api/') and legacy OData ('/_odata') routes from a single external source — the exact extraction path ExfilSquad used against misconfigured Anonymous Users web roles to pull Dataverse records (names, orgs, work emails) behind the PNLD breach. Surfaces bulk record pulls that a normal portal-browsing session would never generate. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete '/_api/', '/_odata' and '/_services/' Power Pages routes plus a 200-status + high-volume shape confirmed by VenariX and Microsoft Learn as the ExfilSquad extraction path; Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because Power Pages/Dataverse HTTP request logs are not shipped to endpoint EDR or AWS telemetry — the signal lives only in web-tier logs. Cross-checked VenariX, Microsoft Power Platform governance blog, and Microsoft Learn Web API overview. Cross-checked against: • https://venarix.com/blog/exfilsquad-targets-misconfigured-microsoft-power-pages-portals • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/configure/web-api-overview • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/blog/power-pages/governance-control-to-disable-anonymous-access-to-dataverse-data-in-power-pages-websites/ • https://appomni.com/ao-labs/microsoft-power-pages-data-exposure-reviewed/
ATT&CKT1213 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized integration/service accounts (Power Automate, ETL) syncing Dataverse through the portal Web API
  • Portal client-side JavaScript issuing many /_api/ calls to render list/grid views in one legitimate session
  • Approved uptime/synthetic monitors (UptimeRobot, Azure Traffic Manager Endpoint Monitor) polling portal pages
  • Search-engine crawlers (Googlebot, bingbot) indexing portal content
  • Your own authorized web/pentest scan of the portal
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Googlebot","bingbot","UptimeRobot","Azure Traffic Manager Endpoint Monitor","PowerAutomate","Microsoft-Flow")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull SampleUrls for the top SrcIpAddr — identify which Dataverse entity sets were read and whether they hold PII (contacts, systemusers, incidents). Geolocate the IP and check if the UA/IP maps to a known integration. 2) CONTAIN: In Power Platform admin, enable the tenant governance control to block unauthenticated Dataverse reads and remove Anonymous Users table permissions / disable the Web API + legacy OData feed on the affected site; validate access from an unauthenticated browser session. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every Power Pages site in the tenant, test each /_api and /_odata route unauthenticated, and review web logs for the same SrcIpAddr/UA hitting other portals.
let lookback = 24h;
let extractionThreshold = 100;   // 100 = bulk-pull floor; a single interactive portal session rarely hits >100 successful /_api calls
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url contains "/_api/" or Url contains "/_odata" or Url contains "/_services/"   // Power Pages Web API + legacy OData feed routes
| extend Status = coalesce(HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseCode)
| where Status == 200
| summarize Requests = count(),
            DistinctUrls = dcount(Url),
            TotalRespBytes = sum(HttpResponseBodyBytes),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 15)
    by SrcIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| where Requests > extractionThreshold
| order by Requests desc
title: Anonymous Bulk Access to Power Pages Web API / OData Dataverse Endpoints
id: 3f2a1c9e-8b47-4d6a-bf21-7c9e5a1d2b30
status: experimental
description: Detects requests to Microsoft Power Pages Web API (/_api/) or legacy OData (/_odata) routes that expose Dataverse table data, as abused by ExfilSquad against misconfigured Anonymous Users web roles (PNLD and related breaches).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/pnld-breach-exposes-uk-police-and.html
  - https://venarix.com/blog/exfilsquad-targets-misconfigured-microsoft-power-pages-portals
  - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/configure/web-api-overview
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1213
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/_api/'
      - '/_odata'
      - '/_services/'
    sc-status: 200
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Authenticated portal users or integration service accounts retrieving records via the Web API
  - Portal client-side JavaScript rendering list/grid pages for a single browsing session
level: medium
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as requests, sum(Web.bytes_out) as total_bytes_out, dc(Web.url) as distinct_urls, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/_api/*" OR Web.url="*/_odata*" OR Web.url="*/_services/*") Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent, Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where requests > 100
| eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), lastTime=strftime(lastTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - requests
| tstats summariesonly=false count as requests, sum(Web.bytes_out) as total_bytes_out, dc(Web.url) as distinct_urls, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/_api/*" OR Web.url="*/_odata*" OR Web.url="*/_services/*") Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent, Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where requests > 100
| eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), lastTime=strftime(lastTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
| sort - requests
Dataverse table enumeration across Power Pages /_api and /_odata entity sets AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single external source touching many distinct Power Pages Web API/OData entity-set names (with a mix of 200 and 401/403 responses) — the reconnaissance step where an actor maps which Dataverse tables are readable under the Anonymous Users web role before extracting them. Distinct pivot from bulk extraction: keys on breadth of tables probed, not request volume. Rationale: Uses the same article-confirmed '/_api/' and '/_odata' routes but pivots on dcount of distinct entity-set names + a 200/401/403 response mix — the behavioral fingerprint of an actor discovering which Dataverse tables the Anonymous Users role exposes. Aggregation/dcount logic means no Sigma (per rules); no Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch because the telemetry is web-tier only. Cross-checked VenariX and Microsoft Learn. Cross-checked against: • https://venarix.com/blog/exfilsquad-targets-misconfigured-microsoft-power-pages-portals • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-pages/configure/web-api-overview • https://appomni.com/ao-labs/microsoft-power-pages-data-exposure-reviewed/
ATT&CKT1595.003 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portal application itself calling several entity sets to render multiple list/grid components in one legitimate session
  • Developers or admins testing Web API table permissions during a portal build/change
  • Authorized security scanners or Power Pages configuration-audit tooling you run yourself
  • Bot/crawler traffic touching multiple portal API paths
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Googlebot","bingbot","UptimeRobot","Azure Traffic Manager Endpoint Monitor")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Review EntitySets for the flagged SrcIpAddr — note whether sensitive tables (contact, systemuser, incident, email) returned 200 (exposed) vs 401/403 (locked). Confirm the source is not a sanctioned integration or internal test. 2) CONTAIN: Remove Anonymous Users read permissions from any table that returned 200, disable the legacy OData feed, and enable the tenant-level anonymous-Dataverse-read block; re-test unauthenticated. 3) HUNT: Search other tenant portals for the same SrcIpAddr/UA and pivot to UC-1 to see if enumeration was followed by bulk extraction from the same source.
let lookback = 24h;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url contains "/_api/" or Url contains "/_odata"   // Power Pages Web API / legacy OData entity-set access
| extend Status = coalesce(HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseCode)
| extend EntitySet = tostring(extract(@"/_(?:api|odata)/([A-Za-z0-9_]+)", 1, Url))
| where isnotempty(EntitySet)
| summarize DistinctEntitySets = dcount(EntitySet),
            EntitySets = make_set(EntitySet, 40),
            Allowed = countif(Status == 200),
            Denied = countif(Status in (401, 403, 404)),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SrcIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| where DistinctEntitySets >= 5   // 5+ distinct Dataverse tables probed by one source = enumeration, not normal browsing
| order by DistinctEntitySets desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_paths >= 5
| eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), lastTime=strftime(lastTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_paths, values(Web.status) as statuses, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/_api/*" OR Web.url="*/_odata*") by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent, Web.dest

Inbound phishing leveraging the PNLD / ExfilSquad breach against named officers AIDelivery Low
Hunts inbound mail whose subject or links reference the PNLD breach lures (PNLD, Police National Legal Database, Ask the Police, ExfilSquad) — the exact follow-on risk UK government guidance flagged, where leaked officer names and work emails make targeted phishing more convincing. Filters out the legitimate breach-notification mail the affected orgs are actually receiving. Rationale: Anchors on the article-specific lure themes (PNLD, Police National Legal Database, Ask the Police, ExfilSquad) that leaked names/work-emails make credible, and explicitly excludes the legitimate pnld.co.uk / ico.org.uk / police.uk breach-notification senders. Low confidence by nature (theme-matching); Sentinel left empty because the provided tenant schema has no EmailEvents-equivalent with reliable Subject content, and Falcon/CloudWatch don't carry O365 mailflow. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/pnld-breach-exposes-uk-police-and.html • https://venarix.com/blog/exfilsquad-targets-misconfigured-microsoft-power-pages-portals • https://hackread.com/microsoft-power-pages-misconfigurations-data-leak/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate breach-notification emails from PNLD, ICO or the affected police forces to staff
  • Internal security-awareness / all-staff advisories referencing the PNLD breach
  • News alerts, threat-intel newsletters or vendor advisories mentioning ExfilSquad / PNLD
  • Journalist or partner enquiries about the incident
Suppression filter
and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "pnld.co.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "ico.org.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "police.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "nationalcrimeagency.gov.uk"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Verify the SenderMailFromDomain and authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC in AuthenticationDetails) — legitimate PNLD/ICO notices will pass and come from expected domains; lookalike or failing-auth senders with a link are suspect. Inspect Url/UrlDomain for credential-harvest pages. 2) CONTAIN: Soft-delete/quarantine confirmed malicious messages tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender domain and URL, and warn the targeted recipients not to click. 3) HUNT: Pivot on UrlClickEvents for the same URL to find who clicked, and search for the same sender/URL across other affected police-force tenants.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where Subject has_any ("PNLD","Police National Legal Database","Ask the Police","ExfilSquad") or Subject has_all ("data breach","police")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | take 0) on $left.NetworkMessageId == $left.NetworkMessageId
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| where SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "pnld.co.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "ico.org.uk" and SenderMailFromDomain !endswith "police.uk"   // strip the genuine breach-notice senders
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryAction, PhishConfidenceLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the

EmailEvents

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

| sort - files

StepSecurity
2026-08-03 2 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An AI agent published a malicious package to PyPI and 15 systems ran it within an hour. What Anthropic's incident means for supply chain security.

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

N-able Says Attackers Take Over N-central Servers After Initial Fix Proves Incomplete

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 11 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

N-able said attackers exploited an authentication bypass in N-central to gain remote administrative access and reach the customer systems managed through those servers. Its first fix was incomplete. CVE-2026-18577 affects N-central builds prior to 2026.3.1.7. N-able shipped build 2026.3.1.7 on August 2 as the first unaffected version. N-central is the remote monitoring and management platform

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint contact with N-able-published attacker IPs / Synology QuickConnect C2 domains · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] N-able Take Control agent spawning shell / process-enumeration on managed endpoint
Cloudflared tunnel registered as a Windows service on N-central-managed endpoint AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step N-able attributed to this campaign: after reaching a managed endpoint via Take Control, attackers install cloudflared and register it as a service named 'Cloudflared' so an outbound tunnel to Cloudflare's edge survives reboot and outlives the revoked N-central route. Fires on cloudflared executed with service-install / tunnel-run arguments. Rationale: Uses N-able's named IOC (a service called 'Cloudflared') plus cloudflared's real service-install/tunnel-run/--token CLI. Corroborated by Huntress and N-able's Aug-2 advisory describing tunnels registered as services on managed endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-central-security-update-august-2-2026 • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/critical-n-able-n-central-flaw-actively-exploited/
ATT&CKT1572 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP or internal IT legitimately deploying Cloudflare Tunnel for remote access to a server
  • DevOps registering cloudflared as a service for Cloudflare Access (SSH/RDP over tunnel)
  • Cloudflare Zero Trust WARP connector rollout
  • Cloudflared auto-update service re-registering itself
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","cloudflare-warp.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "cloudflarewarp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is an N-central-managed endpoint and whether Cloudflare Tunnel is a sanctioned tool there; pull the InitiatingProcess parent chain and the token/tunnel ID from the command line. 2) Contain: stop and delete the Cloudflared service, kill cloudflared.exe, and block outbound to Cloudflare tunnel endpoints from that host; isolate if the parent is a Take Control/N-central agent. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints under the same N-central/partner account for the Cloudflared service, svchost.exe in Documents, and connections to the published attacker IPs/domains; upgrade N-central to 2026.3.1.7.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "cloudflared"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("service install", "tunnel run", "--token")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "cloudflared"
| where CommandLine has_any ("service install", "tunnel run", "--token")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cloudflared Tunnel Installed as Service (N-central Compromise)
id: 6f2b1c94-3d7a-4e1b-9a2c-8f0e1d5c7b21
description: Detects cloudflared executed with service-install or tunnel-run arguments, the persistence technique N-able attributed to N-central (CVE-2026-18577) exploitation.
references:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\cloudflared.exe OR *\\Cloudflared.exe) OR @CommandLine:*cloudflared*) @CommandLine:(*"service install"* OR *"tunnel run"* OR *--token*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/cloudflared\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/cloudflared/i) | CommandLine=/(service\s+install|tunnel\s+run|--token)/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
