| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*cloudflared*" AND (Processes.process="*service install*" OR Processes.process="*tunnel run*" OR Processes.process="*--token*")) OR Processes.process_name="cloudflared.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
svchost.exe masquerading from a user Documents folder (N-central attacker drop) AIInstallation High
Hunts N-able's explicit IOC: a file named svchost.exe living in a user's Documents folder. Genuine svchost.exe only ever runs from System32/SysWOW64, so any svchost.exe process launched from \Users\*\Documents\ on an N-central-managed endpoint is high-fidelity masquerading tied to this intrusion. Rationale: Directly encodes N-able's stated IOC 'svchost.exe in users' Documents folders'. Real svchost.exe only lives in System32/SysWOW64, so the Documents path is a near-zero-FP masquerade signal cross-confirmed by Huntress and gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-central-security-update-august-2-2026 • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/critical-n-able-n-central-flaw-actively-exploited/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware analyst intentionally copying svchost.exe to Documents in a lab
  • Backup/restore tooling staging a captured svchost.exe into a user profile
  • Incident-response collection tool copying system binaries into a Documents-based evidence folder
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the Documents\svchost.exe and compare to the real System32 svchost.exe; check signer, InitiatingProcess parent, and whether the host is N-central-managed. 2) Contain: kill the process, quarantine the file, and isolate the endpoint if the parent chain traces to a Take Control/N-central agent. 3) Hunt: across the partner/N-central fleet, look for the Cloudflared service, connections to the published IPs/domains, and other svchost.exe outside System32; preserve ui_access_control.log and BASupSrvc_*.log.gz.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\" and FolderPath has @"\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\Users\" and NewProcessName has @"\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\users\\[^\\]+\\documents\\.*svchost\.exe$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())

Endpoint contact with N-able-published attacker IPs / Synology QuickConnect C2 domains AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network egress or DNS resolution from managed endpoints to the six attacker IPs N-able published and the three Synology/QuickConnect domains Huntress published (mousears.synology.me, wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to, who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to). Domains are high-fidelity; IPs are lower (Huntress flagged four as Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes) so correlate with N-central/endpoint context. Rationale: Ships N-able's six published IPs and Huntress's three QuickConnect domains together. Only shipped because a second source (Huntress) confirmed the domains and characterised the IPs; the IP clause is marked lower-fidelity because four are shared VPN exit nodes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://www.n-able.com/blog/n-central-security-update-august-2-2026 • https://gbhackers.com/critical-n-able-n-central-flaw-actively-exploited/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090 T1008
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated users behind Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes that share the four flagged IPs (benign VPN traffic)
  • A legitimate Synology NAS owner in the environment whose QuickConnect ID coincidentally matches (extremely unlikely for the exact three)
  • Threat-intel or sandbox appliance deliberately resolving the IOCs for enrichment
  • Security researcher browsing to the domains for analysis
Suppression filter
// For IP-only matches, prioritise hosts that also resolved one of the three QuickConnect domains or ran cloudflared/svchost-in-Documents
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and host; separate DNS hits on the three domains (treat as high-confidence) from IP-only hits (validate against VPN-exit-node context and N-central UI/endpoint logs). 2) Contain: block the domains and IPs at the proxy/firewall, isolate hosts with domain resolutions, and capture the initiating process for analysis. 3) Hunt: on any confirmed host, look for the Cloudflared service, svchost.exe in Documents, and Take Control-driven process enumeration; expand across the same N-central partner account.
let badIPs = dynamic(["173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181","68.235.46.214"]);
let badDomains = dynamic(["mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (badIPs) or RemoteUrl in~ (badDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let badIPs = dynamic(["173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181","68.235.46.214"]);
let badDomains = dynamic(["mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP in (badIPs) | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceProduct, Activity),
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name in~ (badDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

N-able Take Control agent spawning shell / process-enumeration on managed endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-compromise behaviour Huntress observed: attackers pivoting through the N-central Take Control agent (GetSupportService_N-Central / BASupSrvc.exe) into a shell that enumerates running processes before disconnecting. Targets the Take Control agent as parent of cmd/powershell or process-discovery LOLBins, the article's stated hands-on-keyboard activity. Rationale: Encodes Huntress's stated detection surface (Take Control agent GetSupportService_N-Central/BASupSrvc) and the observed post-compromise action (enumerating running processes). Parent=Take Control agent + child=shell/discovery LOLBin is the article's specific hands-on-keyboard shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/n-able-vulnerability-exploitation • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html
ATT&CKT1219 T1057 T1078.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MSP technician running tasklist/whoami during a sanctioned Take Control support session
  • Take Control agent self-diagnostics spawning cmd.exe
  • Scheduled health-check scripts invoked through the N-able agent
  • Genuine helpdesk troubleshooting of a hung process on the endpoint
Suppression filter
// Suppress sessions confirmed against an approved technician identity in ui_access_control.log; keep any tied to mspsupport@n-able.com or an unknown operator for review
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the process time with ui_access_control.log and C:\ProgramData\GetSupportService_N-Central\Logs\BASupSrvc_*.log.gz and check whether the session maps to a legitimate technician or an apparent N-able support identity such as mspsupport@n-able.com. 2) Contain: if the session is unauthorised, terminate the Take Control session, isolate the endpoint, and disable/rotate the implicated N-central operator account. 3) Hunt: on that host and its siblings under the same N-central account, look for the Cloudflared service, svchost.exe in Documents, and beaconing to the published IPs/domains; ensure N-central is on 2026.3.1.7.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("BASupSrvc", "GetSupportService")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","tasklist.exe","qprocess.exe","whoami.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tasklist","Get-Process","query process")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("BASupSrvc", "GetSupportService")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","tasklist.exe","qprocess.exe","whoami.exe") or CommandLine has_any ("tasklist","Get-Process","query process")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-18556", "CVE-2026-18577")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-18556", "CVE-2026-18577")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 12 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Three high-severity security flaws have been disclosed in Hugging Face's Diffusers library that could allow crafted model repositories to stealthily execute arbitrary code on machines that load it, opening the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain to security risk. "These vulnerabilities are bypassing trust_remote_code, the safeguard designed to stop unreviewed code from running in the

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Unexpected Python file staged in Hugging Face model cache/snapshot (FaceHugger) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Python process spawns shell/LOLBin child in Diffusers/Hugging Face context · [LLM] Vulnerable Hugging Face Diffusers (< 0.38.0) exposure inventory (FaceHugger) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound network from Python/Diffusers process to non-Hugging-Face host · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Unexpected Python file staged in Hugging Face model cache/snapshot (FaceHugger) AIDelivery High
Hunts crafted custom-pipeline code (e.g. None.py, pipeline.py) written into a downloaded Hugging Face model snapshot or hub cache by a Python/huggingface-cli process. FaceHugger (CVE-2026-44827/44513) delivers RCE by planting a .py the trust_remote_code gate never inspected — the maintainers' own workaround is to scan snapshots for unexpected *.py under component subdirs (unet/, scheduler/, vae/). Rationale: Uses the article's concrete artefacts: the None.py filename from CVE-2026-44827, the pipeline.py custom-pipeline flow, and the maintainer workaround's component subdirs (unet/, scheduler/, vae/) under the HF cache/snapshot path — a .py landing there is never a legitimate model weight. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hugging-face-diffusers-trust/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/diffusers/CVE-2026-44827/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/diffusers-rce-via-none-py-bypass-cve-2026-44827/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom-pipeline model repos that ship an intended pipeline.py loaded with trust_remote_code=True by ML engineers
  • A data-science team vendoring their own Diffusers pipeline into a local snapshot for reproducibility
  • Model conversion/quant tooling writing helper .py scripts into a cache-adjacent working dir
  • Security researchers reproducing the PoC in a sandbox
  • huggingface-cli download of a community pipeline the org has already reviewed and allowlisted
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\allowlisted_pipelines\\") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-ml-ci"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the staged .py (None.py/pipeline.py) and read it — look for os.system/subprocess/exec/eval, network calls, or obfuscated blobs; identify the source repo from the models--<org>--<name> folder. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, kill any child process spawned by the loading python.exe, and block the source repo/org at the proxy; pin the host's Diffusers to >=0.38.0. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId/aid for python spawning shells (UC2) and outbound to non-HF hosts (UC3), and search other hosts that pulled the same models-- repo.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".py"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.cache\huggingface\", "/.cache/huggingface/", @"\huggingface\hub\", "/huggingface/hub/", "models--")
| where FolderPath has_any ("snapshots", @"\unet\", "/unet/", @"\scheduler\", "/scheduler/", @"\vae\", "/vae/", @"\text_encoder\", "/text_encoder/") or FileName in~ ("None.py","pipeline.py")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","huggingface-cli.exe","huggingface-cli")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".py"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.cache\huggingface\", "/.cache/huggingface/", @"\huggingface\hub\", "/huggingface/hub/", "models--")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("snapshots", "/unet/", @"\unet\", "/scheduler/", @"\scheduler\", "/vae/", "/text_encoder/") or TargetFileName in~ ("None.py","pipeline.py")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","huggingface-cli")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Unexpected Python File Staged in Hugging Face Model Cache (FaceHugger)
id: 6b2a1e94-7c3d-4f10-9a2e-3d5b8c1f7a20
description: Detects a .py file (e.g. None.py or pipeline.py) written into a Hugging Face model snapshot or hub cache directory, the delivery vector for the FaceHugger trust_remote_code bypass (CVE-2026-44827 / CVE-2026-44513).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hugging-face-diffusers-flaws-could-let.html
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/diffusers/CVE-2026-44827/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\huggingface\hub\'
      - '\.cache\huggingface\'
      - 'models--'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.py'
  condition: selection_path and selection_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\huggingface\hub\* OR *\HuggingFace\hub\* OR *\.cache\huggingface\* OR *models--*) @TargetFilename:(*.py OR *None.py OR *pipeline.py)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\.cache[\\\/]huggingface|huggingface[\\\/]hub|models--)/i
| TargetFileName=/\.py$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(python|huggingface-cli)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path IN ("*\\huggingface\\hub\\*","*/.cache/huggingface/*","*models--*")) Filesystem.file_name IN ("*.py") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where (like(file_path,"%snapshots%") OR like(file_path,"%unet%") OR like(file_path,"%scheduler%") OR like(file_path,"%vae%") OR like(file_path,"%text_encoder%") OR file_name="None.py" OR file_name="pipeline.py") | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path IN ("*\\huggingface\\hub\\*","*/.cache/huggingface/*","*models--*")) Filesystem.file_name IN ("*.py") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where (like(file_path,"%snapshots%") OR like(file_path,"%unet%") OR like(file_path,"%scheduler%") OR like(file_path,"%vae%") OR like(file_path,"%text_encoder%") OR file_name="None.py" OR file_name="pipeline.py") | sort - lastTime
Python process spawns shell/LOLBin child in Diffusers/Hugging Face context AIExploitation High
Hunts a python/pythonw process (the Diffusers loader) spawning a command shell or LOLBin, the RCE payoff of a FaceHugger custom_pipeline bypass. Scoped to loader command lines referencing diffusers/DiffusionPipeline/from_pretrained/custom_pipeline/huggingface so it fires on model-load-triggered execution rather than routine scripting. Rationale: Pairs the article's execution vector (custom_pipeline/from_pretrained loading arbitrary code) with a concrete parent(python)->child(shell/LOLBin) tree, and constrains the parent command line to Diffusers/HF tokens so it is article-specific rather than generic python scripting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hugging-face-diffusers-trust/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/diffusers/CVE-2026-44827/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ML pipeline legitimately shelling out to nvidia-smi/git/ffmpeg during model load
  • Jupyter/VS Code notebook where a data scientist runs !cmd style commands from a diffusers cell
  • MLOps orchestration (Airflow/Prefect) invoking curl or bash post-download hooks
  • setup.py/build steps that compile CUDA kernels via cmd during first import
  • Automated model-eval harness spawning powershell to move output files
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","bash","sh") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("nvidia-smi","ffmpeg","git rev-parse") and AccountName in~ ("svc-ml-ci"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the parent python command line; determine if the shell invocation is expected for that pipeline (build/eval hook) or unexplained. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and freeze the loaded models-- repo/snapshot for analysis; block the repo at the proxy. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for the staged malicious .py (UC1) and non-HF egress from python (UC3); sweep the fleet for the same repo name and the same child command line.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","bash","sh")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("diffusers","DiffusionPipeline","from_pretrained","custom_pipeline","huggingface")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has "python"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","/bash","/sh")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("diffusers","DiffusionPipeline","from_pretrained","custom_pipeline","huggingface")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound network from Python/Diffusers process to non-Hugging-Face host AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a python interpreter in a Diffusers/HF context making an outbound connection to any public host that is NOT Hugging Face infrastructure or a package index. After a FaceHugger RCE the attacker code runs inside the loader process; its first beacon/exfil will egress from python.exe to attacker infrastructure, not to huggingface.co. Rationale: Anchored on the article's statement that the RCE runs inside the model-loading process; python egressing to anything other than HF CDN/PyPI while a diffusers load is in flight is a high-signal post-exploitation pivot. HF CDN hosts (cdn-lfs, xethub) are allowlisted to avoid benign model-download noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hugging-face-diffusers-trust/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Diffusers loading a model whose config pulls auxiliary weights from a non-HF mirror (e.g. an S3 bucket or civitai)
  • Telemetry/metrics libraries (wandb, huggingface_hub analytics) beaconing to their own SaaS endpoints
  • pip/conda resolving a dependency from a private/internal index not in the allowlist
  • A model card referencing an external image/asset CDN fetched during load
  • Corporate proxy/PAC causing python traffic to appear destined for the proxy host
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("wandb.ai","sentry.io") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-ml-ci"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the destination (domain age, reputation, ASN) and confirm whether the python command line and loaded repo explain the connection; capture bytes-out. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress, isolate the host, and preserve the loaded snapshot; rotate any secrets reachable from that process. 3) Hunt: correlate to the staged .py (UC1) and shell spawn (UC2) on the same host and time window; sweep the org for other hosts beaconing to the same destination or loading the same models-- repo.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","cdn-lfs.huggingface.co","cdn-lfs.hf.co","xethub.hf.co","cas-bridge.xethub.hf.co","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","githubusercontent.com"))
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("diffusers","DiffusionPipeline","from_pretrained","custom_pipeline","huggingface")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","cdn-lfs.huggingface.co","cdn-lfs.hf.co","xethub.hf.co","cas-bridge.xethub.hf.co","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","githubusercontent.com"))

Vulnerable Hugging Face Diffusers (< 0.38.0) exposure inventory (FaceHugger) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running a Diffusers version below 0.38.0 or explicitly flagged for the FaceHugger CVEs, the exploitable population for CVE-2026-44827/45804/44513. Exposure-management pivot to prioritise patching of the trust_remote_code bypass before it is weaponised. Rationale: Uses the exact fixed version (0.38.0, released early May 2026) and the three CVE IDs from the article/GitLab advisory; a straight exposure query that scopes remediation to the genuinely vulnerable hosts with zero behavioural FP. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/diffusers/CVE-2026-44827/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hugging-face-diffusers-trust/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A host pinned to <0.38.0 but which never calls DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained with custom_pipeline (lower real risk)
  • TVM reporting a stale inventory entry after the package was already upgraded in a venv
  • A vendored/forked diffusers with a non-standard version string that back-ports the fix
  • Air-gapped build agent that only ever loads locally-audited snapshots
  • Duplicate rows where the same package is inventoried under multiple Python environments
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hosts by internet exposure and whether they load third-party HF repos; confirm the reported version against the actual venv/site-packages. 2) Contain: patch to Diffusers >= 0.38.0; where patching lags, enforce the maintainer workaround (only from_pretrained on audited local snapshots, never point custom_pipeline at a different Hub repo). 3) Hunt: on any host that cannot patch immediately, deploy UC1-UC3 as compensating detections and review recent model pulls for unexpected .py files.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-08-01 4 use cases 3 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Galaxy Research mapped the sweep and tied it to a firmware flaw in Coldcard, the Bitcoin-only hardware wallet made by Canadian firm Coinkite. Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

Rails patches critical Active Storage flaw with RCE potential

BleepingComputer
2026-08-01 6 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A critical vulnerability in the Active Storage framework can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a Rails application, and potentially escalate to remote code execution (RCE). [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) · [LLM] Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rails app worker spawning shell or network child (KindaRails2Shell RCE)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rails/Ruby worker reading secret_key_base and credential files post-upload (CVE-2026-66066) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated traffic to Rails Active Storage upload and variant/representation endpoints, the exploitation surface for CVE-2026-66066 (KindaRails2Shell) where a crafted image drives libvips into an arbitrary-file-read. Surfaces sources that both submit uploads and request server-side image processing so an analyst can triage the file-read primitive. Rationale: Uses the canonical Rails Active Storage route prefixes (/rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, /representations/, /blobs/, /disk/) — corroborated by Rapid7/Ethiack as the direct-upload + variant-processing surface. Technical PoC strings were withheld by the researchers, so this is a triage hunt on the exploit surface rather than a signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading avatars/profile pictures and viewing generated thumbnails
  • Load/synthetic monitoring hitting upload endpoints
  • CDN or image-proxy warming Active Storage representations in bulk
  • Mobile app clients using direct_uploads at high volume
  • Security scanners (internal ASM/DAST) probing the same routes
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the raw requests for the top source IPs — check whether they are unauthenticated, whether upload requests are immediately followed by representation/variant requests, and whether responses are anomalously sized (leaked file content). 2) Contain: if libvips <8.13 or the app is unpatched (Rails <7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1), block the source at the WAF/reverse-proxy and enable VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host to UC 'Rails worker sensitive-file access' and 'Rails worker spawning shell/network child' to confirm file-read and RCE.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/rails/active_storage/"
| where Url has_any ("/representations/", "/blobs/", "/direct_uploads", "/disk/")
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(HttpMethod, 10), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| order by LastSeen desc

Rails/Ruby worker reading secret_key_base and credential files post-upload (CVE-2026-66066) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Rails application process (ruby/puma/unicorn/passenger) accessing sensitive secret and environment files — the credential-access step of CVE-2026-66066 where the libvips arbitrary-file-read is used to exfiltrate secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc, .env and /proc/self/environ. High-fidelity because a running web worker should not be reading these at request time. Rationale: Ties the standard Rails secret paths named in the article (secret_key_base, master.key, database/cloud creds in the process environment) to the app-server process identity — a Rails worker reading /proc/self/environ or master.key at runtime is the direct fingerprint of the file-read primitive being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-66066-critical-rails-flaw-exposes-server-files-via-image-uploads/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal app boot reading config/master.key and credentials.yml.enc during initialization (baseline once per deploy/restart)
  • dotenv gems loading .env at startup
  • Config-management/CI tooling templating credential files
  • APM/observability agents enumerating process environment
  • Developer console (rails c) sessions on a jump host
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "FileCreated" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "rails console" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "assets:precompile"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the access is at request-serving time (not process boot) and correlate the host/timestamp with UC1 Active Storage upload traffic within the same window. 2) Contain: treat secret_key_base, DB and Active Storage credentials as compromised — rotate them, rotate the Rails master key, and patch to Rails 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1 with libvips ≥8.13. 3) Hunt: search for forged session cookies / anomalous authenticated sessions and pivot to UC3 for shell/network children of the worker.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where FileName in~ ("credentials.yml.enc", "master.key", "environ", ".env")
    or FolderPath has_any ("/config/credentials", "/proc/self/environ")
| where FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/" and FolderPath !has "/active_storage/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/credentials.yml.enc", "/config/master.key", "/config/credentials/", "/proc/self/environ")
    or TargetFileName =~ ".env"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rails app worker spawning shell or network child (KindaRails2Shell RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the Rails/Ruby application server (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) spawning an unexpected shell or network client (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python, ruby -e) — the RCE execution stage where a forged, secret_key_base-signed serialized payload drives insecure deserialization into command execution on the host. Rationale: A web application worker (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) is not expected to fork shells or curl/wget at runtime; pairing that specific parent set with shell/network children is the highest-fidelity signal of the deserialization-to-RCE endgame the article and Akamai describe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg/git via system() for background jobs
  • Sidekiq/Resque workers running rake tasks that invoke curl/bash
  • Health-check or entrypoint scripts (bash) launched by the app container
  • Deploy hooks calling shell from within the app process
  • Ruby scripts using backticks for legitimate ops tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert", "identify", "vipsthumbnail", "ffmpeg", "/rake", "sidekiq", "healthcheck"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — reverse-shell one-liners, curl to unknown IPs, or writes to /tmp are strong TP indicators; benign image/rake tooling is FP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, and treat app secrets as compromised (rotate secret_key_base + all DB/cloud creds). 3) Hunt: pull outbound connections from the child, correlate back to the originating Active Storage upload (UC1) and credential-file reads (UC2), and search other Rails hosts for the same parent→child pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "curl", "wget", "nc", "ncat", "python", "python3", "perl")
    or (FileName in~ ("ruby") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh", "/bash", "/dash", "/curl", "/wget", "/nc", "/ncat", "/python", "/perl")
    or (ActingProcessName has "/ruby" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation High
Surfaces internet-facing hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-66066 — libvips before 8.13 (which cannot disable the unfuzzed operations at all) or unpatched Rails Active Storage. Drives pre-exploitation prioritization since public PoCs are already circulating. Rationale: Directly keys on the article's named CVE (CVE-2026-66066) and the libvips 8.13 fix floor; scoping to internet-facing hosts turns the vuln feed into an actionable, prioritized exposure list ahead of the disclosed public PoCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://www.linuxcompatible.org/story/rails-7232-8051-and-8131-active-storage-security-patch-targets-cve202666066
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that use ImageMagick (not libvips) as the Active Storage processor — not actually exploitable
  • Apps that do not accept untrusted image uploads (internal-only) — lower real risk
  • TVM version-string mismatch flagging a backported/distro-patched libvips as vulnerable
  • Rails 6.x using Active Storage defaults (not affected) still flagged by generic version match
  • Decommissioned/quarantined hosts still in inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm it uses the vips processor and accepts untrusted uploads (else de-prioritize), and check internet exposure. 2) Contain: patch Active Storage to 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1, upgrade libvips to ≥8.13, and set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true); apply WAF virtual patch where immediate upgrade isn't possible. 3) Hunt: retro-scan UC1/UC2/UC3 telemetry on every exposed host for prior exploitation before the patch window.

Adform crypto-swap stealer C2/exfil beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint or perimeter connections to the hardcoded attacker server 84.32.102.230 on TCP/7744, the exfil endpoint the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js beacons to on page load (sending victim hostname + path). This IP:port is the single highest-fidelity IOC of the campaign — it exists only in the malicious payload. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the exact exfil IP:port confirmed across the article and second sources (BleepingComputer, Beaumont/DoublePulsar). A raw-IP non-standard-port destination with no legitimate business use makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/adform-script-crypto-wallet-address-swap/
ATT&CKT1571 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware sandbox detonating the captured sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel scanners or blue-team validation traffic deliberately hitting the IOC
  • IP reallocated to a benign host after the campaign is taken down (validate against WHOIS/first-seen date)
  • Internal proxy or NAT gateway appearing as the source, collapsing many users behind one src_ip
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("sandbox-detonation-01","malware-lab-01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/user and confirm the initiating process is a browser (msedge/chrome/firefox); pull the RemoteUrl/referrer the browser was on to find which affected website served the poisoned script. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at egress/firewall, and instruct the user to clear browser cache (the malicious trackpoint-async.js may persist cached) and verify any crypto wallet addresses recently copied/pasted. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts that both loaded s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js and beaconed to this IP; alert any user who transacted crypto on July 26-27 2026.

Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim: poisoned script load + beacon to attacker IP AIDelivery High
Correlates hosts that loaded the compromised third-party resource s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js with an outbound beacon to 84.32.102.230 on the same host. The script load alone is benign (Adform is loaded by thousands of legitimate sites); the join with the exfil beacon promotes it to a confirmed supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Combines the two confirmed IOCs (poisoned file path s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js and exfil IP 84.32.102.230:7744) on a single host. The join eliminates the massive benign-load noise of Adform being a legitimate ad tag, yielding a high-fidelity supply-chain-victim signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared egress/NAT IP causes an unrelated user's script load to correlate with another user's beacon (validate on managed-host DeviceId join in Defender rather than SrcIpAddr)
  • Proxy that rewrites/caches the Adform URL so the recorded host differs from the beaconing host
  • IOC IP reallocated post-takedown to a benign service
  • Falcon variant relies on DNS to s2.adform.net which is a shared CDN host — treat DNS as a weak loader proxy, the beacon is the anchor
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each correlated host confirm the beacon process is a browser and identify the affected first-party website that embedded the tag. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at egress, force browser cache clear on the host, and reset/verify any crypto wallet addresses the user handled. 3) Hunt: enumerate every user who initiated crypto transactions during the exposure window and review outbound transfers for address substitution; notify affected clients per IR policy.

Exposure scoping: hosts that loaded poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js (Jul 26-28 2026) AIDelivery Medium
IR-scoping hunt that surfaces every managed host which fetched s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js during the compromise window (oldest malicious sample July 26, removed July 27 2026). Used to build the affected-user list for cache-clear guidance and crypto-transaction review, not as a standalone malicious-behaviour alert. Rationale: Anchored on the exact compromised resource path (s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js) and the confirmed malicious window (sample July 26, removed July 27 2026). Deliberately scoped by date because the file was benign before/after — this is an exposure list, not a malicious-behaviour detection, hence hunting tier and high expected FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that loaded the clean, restored trackpoint-async.js after Adform's July 27 fix (mitigated by the date window)
  • Legitimate marketing/ad-ops staff and QA whose job involves the Adform platform
  • Cached copies replayed after the window, skewing timestamps
  • FDR/Falcon variant keys on DNS to shared host s2.adform.net which serves many benign scripts — treat as broad exposure, not confirmation
Suppression filter
| where FirstSeen between (datetime(2026-07-26) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
Response runbook
1) Triage: treat the output as the exposed-population list; prioritise hosts/users known to handle cryptocurrency. 2) Contain: push guidance to clear browser cache (the poisoned file may remain cached) and to re-verify any wallet address before sending funds. 3) Hunt: cross-reference this list against UC 'Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim' (beacon to 84.32.102.230) to separate merely-exposed from confirmed-compromised, and review crypto transactions initiated during the window for address substitution.
